title: What Wine Is
description: What wine is, how it is made in the simplest terms, where it comes from and how to drink it well.
L: The simplest definition, and why it matters
Explain why wine is made from Vitis vinifera
Place a wine's alcohol within the normal range

Wine is the drink you get when yeast ferments the juice of fresh grapes. Drinks made from other fruit, or from rice, can be delicious, but in law they are not simply called wine: in the EU the word on its own is reserved for fermented fresh grapes or grape must.

Almost every wine comes from one species of vine, Vitis vinifera, native to the area between the Black Sea and the Caspian. Within that species there are thousands of varieties, such as Chardonnay or Merlot. Grapes suit wine because a ripe berry holds 20 to 25% sugar, enough acid to stay fresh and the yeast it needs on its own skin.
Species: Vitis vinifera. Variety: the type within it.
Which of these drinks is wine, in the strict sense?
Fermented fresh grape juice is the definition. Fermented apple juice is cider, distilled grape spirit is brandy, and pasteurised juice never fermented, so it has no alcohol.

Most still wines sit between 11 and 14.5% alcohol by volume. Light styles such as Moscato d'Asti can be around 5.5%, while fortified wines like Port reach 19 or 20% because grape spirit is added. The number is always on the label as abv.
A wine labelled 13.5% abv is most likely a fortified wine.
Not true. 13.5% sits comfortably inside the range of ordinary still wine. Fortified wines usually start at 15% and often reach 20%, because spirit is added.
Wine is the fermented juice of fresh grapes
Nearly all wine comes from varieties of Vitis vinifera
Most still wines have 11 to 14.5% alcohol
Explain what yeast does to grape sugar
Put the main winemaking steps in order
Explain why riper grapes give stronger wine

Yeast is a single-celled fungus. In grape juice it eats sugar and gives off alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat. In a still wine the gas escapes into the air. When the sugar runs out, or the alcohol gets too high for the yeast, fermentation stops.
Sugar plus yeast gives alcohol, CO2 and heat

Roughly 17 grams of sugar per litre turn into 1% of alcohol. Juice with 230 g/l of sugar, typical of ripe grapes, can make a wine of about 13.5%. Warm, sunny places ripen grapes further, so their wines tend to be stronger; cool places give lighter, fresher wines.
About 17 g/l of sugar makes 1% alcohol
Unfermented grape juice on its way to becoming wine is called ____.
Must is the juice, with or without skins, before and during fermentation. Lees are the dead yeast left after it, and marc is the pressed skins and seeds.

Every wine follows the same basic path. The grapes are harvested, then crushed or pressed to free the juice. Yeast ferments it. The wine then rests for weeks or years in steel, concrete or oak, which is called maturation. Finally it is bottled.
Put the steps of making a wine in order.
The fruit is picked, the juice is freed, yeast turns it into wine, the wine rests, and only then is it bottled. Maturation always comes after fermentation.
Yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat
Harvest, pressing, fermentation, maturation and bottling come in that order
Riper grapes hold more sugar, so they make stronger wine
The places where vines grow well
Locate the two bands where most wine is made
Explain why vines need a cool season and a warm one
Tell Old World from New World producers

Most wine is made between roughly 30 and 50 degrees of latitude, north and south of the equator. Closer to the equator there is no winter for the vine to rest; further away the summer is too short to ripen the grapes. France, Italy and Spain sit in the northern band; Argentina, South Africa and Australia in the southern one.
Most vineyards lie between 30 and 50 degrees latitude

A vine sleeps through winter, buds in spring, flowers, sets fruit and ripens it through summer. Each step needs the right temperature. Below about 10 degrees Celsius the vine barely grows. Too much heat ripens sugar quickly but burns off acidity, so the best wines come from places with warm days and enough coolness to keep the fruit fresh.
Warm enough to ripen, cool enough to stay fresh
Why is little fine wine made very close to the equator?
There is no cool season for the vine to rest
Grapes cannot grow in the tropics
The vine needs a dormant winter to regulate its yearly cycle. Near the equator it never rests. Grapes do grow there, but making balanced wine is much harder.

Old World means the countries where wine culture began, mainly in Europe, with centuries of rules tied to place. New World means the countries where Europeans planted vines from the 16th century on, such as the United States, Chile, Argentina, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. The terms describe history, not quality.
Old World and New World describe history, not quality
Which of these are New World wine countries?
Chile and New Zealand planted vines with European settlers. Portugal, Italy and Spain have made wine for over two thousand years.
Most wine comes from between 30 and 50 degrees latitude, north and south
The vine needs a winter rest and a summer warm enough to ripen fruit
Old World and New World describe history, not quality
How to enjoy wine and stay well
Work out how much alcohol is in a glass
Explain why food and water change the effect of wine

In the UK, one unit is 10 ml of pure alcohol. A 175 ml glass of 13% wine holds about 2.3 units, and a 750 ml bottle about 10. UK health guidance suggests no more than 14 units a week, spread over several days. Other countries use different measures, but the idea is the same: know how much is in your glass.
Units = volume in ml x abv / 1000

Alcohol is absorbed mostly through the small intestine. A meal slows the stomach, so alcohol reaches the blood more slowly and the peak is lower. The liver breaks down roughly one unit an hour, whatever you do; coffee and cold showers don't speed it up. Water doesn't change that rate, but it helps with thirst and pacing.
The liver clears about one unit an hour
Drinking a strong coffee makes the liver clear alcohol faster.
Not true. Coffee can make you feel more alert, but the liver works at roughly the same speed, about one unit an hour. Only time lowers the alcohol in your blood.
At a tasting, professionals spit. It isn't rude: it lets you taste thirty wines and still judge the last one clearly. Most of what matters, aroma and structure, you get without swallowing.
Roughly how many units are in a 750 ml bottle of 13.5% wine?
750 multiplied by 13.5 and divided by 1000 gives just over 10 units. That's why a bottle shared by two is already a lot for one evening.
A unit is 10 ml of pure alcohol; a bottle of wine holds about 10
Food slows absorption, and only time clears alcohol from the blood
Spitting lets you taste many wines and keep your judgement
Define wine and its alcohol range
Describe how wine is made and where it grows
What makes a drink wine in the strict, legal sense?
The fermentation of fresh grapes or must
Wine is the fermentation of fresh grapes or grape must. The alcohol level describes most wines but doesn't define them, and distillation makes spirit, not wine.
Put the winemaking steps in order.
Fermentation turns juice into wine; maturation is the rest that follows, before bottling.
Grapes from a warmer place usually make a wine with more alcohol.
Yes. More heat and sun means more sugar in the berry, and more sugar becomes more alcohol, about 1% for every 17 g/l.
Which of these are New World wine countries?
Argentina, South Africa and Australia planted vines with European settlers. Spain and Germany are part of the Old World, where wine culture began.
The liver clears roughly ____ unit of alcohol per hour.
About one unit an hour. Coffee, water and fresh air don't change that speed.
Wine is fermented fresh grape juice, usually 11 to 14.5% alcohol
Harvest, pressing, fermentation, maturation and bottling make every wine
Most wine grows between 30 and 50 degrees latitude, in the Old and New Worlds
Know the units in your glass, eat, and spit when tasting
